Beyond Parallel Sampling: Diverse Query Initialization for Agentic Search

Sidhaarth Murali Affiliation:  Carnegie Mellon University, United States Email: ssmurali@andrew.cmu.edu    João Coelho Affiliation:  Carnegie Mellon University, United States Affiliation:  Instituto Superior Técnico and INESC-ID, University of Lisbon, Portugal    Jingjie Ning Affiliation:  Carnegie Mellon University, United States    João Magalhães Affiliation:  NOVA LINCS, NOVA School of Science and Technology, Portugal    Bruno Martins Affiliation:  Instituto Superior Técnico and INESC-ID, University of Lisbon, Portugal    Chenyan Xiong Affiliation:  Carnegie Mellon University, United States
Abstract

Test-time scaling for agentic search typically increases depth (i.e., more turns and tokens per trajectory) or breadth (i.e., more parallel rollouts). Here we focus on breadth scaling, showing that standard parallel sampling yields diminishing returns, tracing this to query redundancy at the first turn. When models issue similar first queries across rollouts, the threads retrieve overlapping evidence, and subsequent turns are conditioned on this shared retrieval. We address this limitation with DivInit, a training-free intervention at the first turn. Rather than sampling kk independent first queries, DivInit draws nn candidates from a single call, picks k<nk<n diverse seeds, and runs them as parallel trajectories. Across five open-weight models and eight benchmarks, DivInit consistently improves over standard parallel sampling, with average gains of five to seven points on multi-hop QA at matched compute. 11 1 Code available at diverse-query-initialization.

1 Introduction

Test-time scaling has become one of the most reliable ways to improve language model performance on complex tasks without training. On search agents, two practical levers dominate current work. The first, depth, extends a single trajectory through longer chains of thought, more reasoning turns, or more search-and-read iterations  (Wei et al., 2022; Muennighoff et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2023; Li and others, 2025). The second, breadth, runs multiple trajectories in parallel and aggregates their outputs through voting, best-of-NN selection, or related strategies (Wang et al., 2023; Cobbe et al., 2021; Brown et al., 2024; Snell et al., 2024).

In this work, we focus on parallel test-time scaling of search agents (i.e., breadth). We empirically identify an anchor collapse phenomenon in multi-turn agentic search, where the turn-1 query anchors the trajectory and the kk parallel threads collapse onto a single retrieval path. When threads start with similar first queries, overlapping evidence is retrieved, and systems fail in correlated ways. Parallel sampling still outperforms a single sequential trajectory (Li et al., 2026), but the low diversity hints at a suboptimal usage of resources (Figure 1).

While standard parallel scaling launches kk independent threads that often anchor on the same turn-1 query, one can instead choose a diverse starting set before any thread runs. The rest of the search agent would be unchanged, making this intervention compatible with any agentic search loop. We name this approach DivInit, sampling nn candidate queries from a single shared call, picking k<nk<n through Maximal Marginal Relevance (MMR) (Carbonell and Goldstein, 1998), and running one trajectory per chosen query.

We evaluate DivInit on five open-weight models across eight benchmarks covering multi-hop QA and long-horizon reasoning. Results show that DivInit consistently improves over standard parallel sampling at matched compute, with average gains of five to seven points on multi-hop QA. The improvement grows with model size on most datasets, suggesting a capacity floor below which models cannot act productively on varied first queries. Moreover, diversity at turn 1 is sufficient on its own, and extending the pool selection to later turns yields little benefit, since the first turn separation carries through subsequent retrieval.

2 Related Work

Test-time Scaling.

Scaling inference-time compute without retraining has proven effective across reasoning and retrieval tasks, through approaches such as chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al., 2022), budget forcing (Muennighoff et al., 2025), process-reward supervision (Lightman et al., 2023; Uesato et al., 2022), self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023), or best-of-NN selection (Cobbe et al., 2021). For long-horizon agentic tasks, AggAgent (Lee et al., 2026) shows that treating parallel trajectories as an interactive environment outperforms voting and answer-concatenation baselines. DivInit addresses a different part of the same problem: rather than improving aggregation after trajectories complete, it diversifies where they start.

Agentic Search.

ReAct (Yao et al., 2023) introduced the thought-action loop for tool-augmented agents, and IRCoT (Trivedi et al., 2023) extended this to multi-hop retrieval. A separate line trains agents via outcome or process rewards (Jin and others, 2025; Chen and others, 2025; Song and others, 2025; Sun and others, 2025; Wen et al., 2026; Anonymous, 2026). DivInit changes only the distribution from which the first query is drawn, before the loop runs, and is compatible with any of the above.

Diversity in Generation and Retrieval.

Diverse beam search (Vijayakumar et al., 2016), nucleus sampling (Holtzman et al., 2020), maximal marginal relevance (Carbonell and Goldstein, 1998), and determinantal point processes (Kulesza and Taskar, 2012; Chen et al., 2018) promote diversity within a single generation or retrieval call. DivInit operates across parallel agent threads at the query level, directly spreading the retrieval neighborhoods each thread will explore.

3 Anchor Collapse in Agentic Search

Agent Setup.

We build on the ReAct-style search agent of Li et al. (2026). Given a question qq, the agent iteratively issues search queries, retrieves the top-NN documents, and decides whether to continue searching or commit to an answer. Each trajectory runs for at most TT turns. Standard parallel sampling draws kk independent trajectories for the same question under temperature τ\tau.

Anchor Collapse.

To characterize interaction diversity across the kk trajectories of a question, we measure two quantities. Query Pairwise Distance (QPD) is the mean pairwise Jaccard distance among tokens from turn-1 queries, where higher QPD indicates that trajectories initialize from distinct retrieval directions. Document overlap is the mean pairwise Jaccard similarity between retrieved document sets, where higher overlap indicates that trajectories consume largely identical evidence despite surface-level query variation.

A preliminary study of standard parallel sampling on the GAIA benchmark (Mialon et al., 2024) shows that these quantities track pass@4 outcome (Figure 2). Questions where all trajectories fail (pass@4 ={=} 0) cluster at low QPD and high document overlap, whereas questions with at least one successful trajectory (pass@4 ={=} 1) show a secondary mode with higher QPD and lower overlap.

We hypothesize that this behavior arises from the sequential dependency structure of agentic retrieval. Because each turn conditions on previously retrieved evidence, trajectories with similar turn-1 retrieval actions tend to remain coupled throughout the search process. Early retrieval decisions therefore anchor subsequent reasoning and evidence acquisition, causing the kk trajectories to collapse onto a narrow region of the search space. We refer to this phenomenon as anchor collapse.

As an example, consider a GAIA question asking for the NASA award number supporting a specific author’s work, linked from a Universe Today article. Under standard parallel sampling, all four trajectories issue identical queries packing every entity into one search (turn-1 QPD 0.098), retrieve the same wrong award number from a different paper, and exhaust their budget without finding the target record. A full trace is provided in Appendix C.

4 DivInit: Diverse Query Initialization

The diagnostic in Section 3 identified low turn-1 QPD as a predictor of failure, i.e., threads that issue near-identical first queries tend to retrieve overlapping evidence and collapse onto a single trajectory. Next we describe DivInit, which aims to control this behavior by oversampling queries in the first turn, and selecting a diverse subset.

Procedure.

The intervention is restricted to the first turn. While standard parallel sampling has each of kk threads generate its own turn-1 query independently, we draw a pool 𝒞\mathcal{C} of n>kn>k candidate queries in a single LLM call at temperature τ\tau. We select kk from 𝒞\mathcal{C} via MMR (Carbonell and Goldstein, 1998), initializing the selected set SS with the pair of candidates at maximum pairwise distance and adding subsequent picks as follows:

c⋆=arg​maxc∈𝒞∖S⁡[(1−λ)​mins∈S​dJ​(c,s)−λ​dJ​(c,q)],c^{\star}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{c\in\mathcal{C}\setminus S}\left[(1-\lambda)\min_{s\in S}d_{J}(c,s)-\lambda\,d_{J}(c,q)\right], (1)

where dJd_{J} is the token-level Jaccard distance, and qq is the original question. We stop when |S|=k|S|=k and run one thread per selected candidate.

Compute Overhead.

The shared pool replaces the kk independent turn-1 LLM calls of standard sampling with a single call that emits nn candidates in one decoding pass, consolidating kk prefills into one at the cost of a longer output. From turn 2, the two methods are identical, so the total cost is 1+k⁡(T−1)1+k(T{-}1) calls, k−1k{-}1 fewer than standard’s k​TkT.

5 Experimental Setup

We evaluate on five open-weight models: Qwen3 (1.7B, 4B, 8B) (Yang and others, 2025) and Gemma3 (4B, 12B) (Kamath and others, 2025), all served locally via vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023). Benchmarks span two groups. First, multi-hop question answering (HotpotQA, MuSiQue, 2WikiMHQA, Bamboogle, FRAMES), for which the agent searches over a local Wiki18 BM25 index (Jin et al., 2025). Second, larger models are also evaluated on open-web reasoning (GAIA, HLE, WebWalker), searching the live web via SERPER (Serper, 2025). We sample 500 questions per benchmark, except for GAIA which uses the full 103-question validation split.

The agent runs T=8T{=}8 turns at k=4k{=}4 threads and temperature τ=1.0\tau{=}1.0. Retrieval returns the textual content of the top 10 documents per query. For DivInit (Eq. 1), we draw n=16n{=}16 candidates in the first turn, and set λ=0\lambda=0 for MMR. Prompts are detailed in Appendix A.1.

6 Experiments

In this section, we measure the empirical gains of DivInit over standard parallel sampling, and analyze the query-level patterns that drive them.

6.1 Empirical Results

Table 1 compares DivInit against standard parallel sampling under a fixed token budget. Results show that DivInit improves on nearly every cell. On the open-web group, WebWalker carries the largest improvements (six to seven points across all three models). While the table shows pass@44, the results also hold for k=8k=8 (Figures 5 and 6 of Appendix B.2) and carry through to pass@1 aggregation under AggAgent (Lee et al., 2026) (Appendix B.3). DivInit only differs from the standard parallel scaling strategy on the first turn. A wall-clock time comparison of both is provided in Appendix B.4.

Results also show that improvement scales with model size. Qwen3 averages move from Δ=2.8\Delta{=}2.8 at 1.7B to Δ=7.4\Delta{=}7.4 at 8B. Notably, the 1.7B numbers point to a capacity floor below which query diversification yields limited benefits.

Figure 3 sweeps τ∈{0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0}\tau\in\{0.5,1.0,1.5,2.0\} for standard parallel sampling, with DivInit at τ=1.0\tau{=}1.0 as reference. Performance tends to improve with temperature, but saturates below DivInit, confirming that sampling noise is not a substitute for explicit diversity selection.

6.2 Qualitative Analysis

Figure 4 shows that standard parallel sampling concentrates turn-1 queries near low QPD values (≈0.2\approx 0.2), while DivInit shifts them toward high diversity (≈0.85\approx 0.85). To test if this separation persists beyond the first turn, we measure Across-Thread Distance (ATD), i.e. the mean pairwise Jaccard distance between tokens in queries from different threads, pooled across all turns.

Questions with higher turn-1 QPD tend to exhibit higher ATD, with positive correlation in both conditions (ρstd=0.42\rho_{\text{std}}{=}0.42, ρDivInit=0.35\rho_{\text{DivInit}}{=}0.35). This further solidifies that turn-1 retrieval acts as a trajectory anchor, i.e., once threads retrieve different evidence early, subsequent reasoning and search remain separated with little additional intervention. Figures 7 and 8 of Appendix B.2 show this pattern across the full grid of benchmarks and models.

6.3 Ablations

Extent of diversification.

DivInit applies pool selection only at turn 1. With Qwen3-8B, extending it to turns 1 through NN for N∈{1,…,8}N\in\{1,...,8\} yields no gain on the open-web benchmarks (Table 2). This matches the observations from §6.2, where early trajectory separation persists throughout later retrieval turns without additional intervention.

Diversity strategy.

DivInit selects kk queries from the pool of nn via MMR with λ\lambda=0, which maximizes the minimum pairwise distance in the selected set. On GAIA with Qwen3-8B, this scores 34.0 pass@4. Setting λ∈{0.5,0.75}\lambda\in\{0.5,0.75\} adds weight to similarity between each candidate and the original question, and drops performance to 30–31, indicating that the LLM-generated pool is already on-topic. Uniform random selection from the same pool scores 27.2, below all MMR variants.

7 Conclusions and Future Work

We identified anchor collapse as a failure mode of standard parallel sampling within agentic search systems, where kk threads converge onto near-identical first queries, retrieve overlapping evidence, and fail in correlated ways. We also proposed DivInit as a training-free fix that oversamples a shared candidate pool of queries and selects a maximally diverse subset before any thread runs. Across five open-weight models and eight benchmarks, the DivInit intervention improves over standard parallel sampling at matched compute, with gains of five to seven points on multi-hop QA.

The results suggest that standard breadth scaling underutilizes inference-time compute by allocating rollout budget to correlated trajectories. The same issue may arise in RL training: in group-based methods such as GRPO, near-identical search trajectories produce low-variance rollout groups and weak learning signals (Singh et al., 2026; Anonymous, 2026). Diversifying trajectory initialization before group formation is a natural next step. A complementary direction is aggregation. DivInit maximizes thread pool diversity but reports pass@kk, while exploiting the structural diversity of the pool to produce a single answer remains open.

Limitations

The pass@kk metric corresponds to the ceiling of what the thread pool can achieve, not the accuracy of any single answer the system would produce in deployment. We also report single-answer accuracy under AggAgent (Lee et al., 2026) in Appendix B.3 and find that diversification gains transfer to pass@1, but closing the remaining gap to pass@kk is an open problem.

Anchor collapse is characterized here for search agents, where the turn-1 decision is a query string and its downstream effect is observable through retrieved documents. Whether the same failure mode arises in other domains, such as tool-use and code, is not addressed in this work.

Ethical Considerations

All the evaluation datasets and pre-trained models used in our experiments are publicly available for research usage. We will provide the source code that allows for reproduction of the results.

By using large pre-trained language models, we acknowledge inherent biases embedded within the models, which may perpetuate or amplify societal biases present in the training data.

Appendix A Reproducibility Details

A.1 Prompts

We use two agent prompts and one pool-generation prompt. All three are reproduced verbatim below (placeholders in curly braces are filled at run time). The multi-hop QA agent uses a ReAct loop with <thought>, <search>, and <answer> actions. The open-web agent adds a <summary> action to compress prior <information> blocks within longer trajectories. The pool-generation prompt is invoked once at turn 1 in every DivInit run to produce the candidate pool of n=16n{=}16 queries.

A.2 Evaluation Protocol

All numbers reported in the main paper are evaluated by gpt-4o-mini (temperature 0, max 300 output tokens). For each question, pass@kk is 1 if at least one of the kk candidates is correct, and 0 otherwise. We report the mean over questions. Because the same judge is applied to every condition, any bias affects all methods equally. The total judge cost is approximately $175.

A.3 Infrastructure and Reproducibility

Open-weight models are served locally with vLLM in bf16 with prefix caching enabled on 4×4{\times} NVIDIA L40S GPUs (48 GB VRAM). Per-rollout seeds are derived deterministically from a SHA-256 hash of the question identifier, the run-level seed, and the rollout index. Search backends are queried with up to five retries on transient failures, and retrieved text is truncated at 4,0004{,}000 characters per turn. Total compute is approximately 590 GPU-hours plus $185 in API costs. The Wiki18 backend is fully reproducible, although SERPER search results drift over time, producing 0.1 to 0.3 points of drift on pass@kk across re-runs.

Appendix B Additional Empirical Results

B.1 Pool Size

Table 4 shows results when varying the oversampled pool size nn, reporting pass@4 values. The performance is essentially unchanged across n∈{8,16,32}n\in\{8,16,32\}, while n=4n{=}4 shows a drop, suggesting the pool should be larger than kk.

B.2 Performance Curves

Figures 5 to 8 report QPD and ATD alongside pass@kk curves over k∈{1,4,8}k\in\{1,4,8\} for every (model, dataset) cell in both benchmark groups. The pattern from §3 is consistent across the grid: standard parallel sampling concentrates at low QPD, DivInit at high QPD, and ATD tracks QPD throughout.

B.3 Aggregation Accuracy

Aggregating kk parallel rollouts into a single answer is not a trivial task, with current strategies falling short of the pass@kk ceiling (Li et al., 2026). Our work focuses on pass@kk, leaving aggregation to existing methods. To verify that DivInit’s gains transfer past the oracle regime, we run AggAgent (Lee et al., 2026), a state-of-the-art LLM-based aggregator, on both standard and DivInit trajectories. Table 3 reports the results. When compared to standard parallel sampling DivInit lifts both the pass@4, and AggAgent’s pass@1 metrics. The diversity gain carries through to single-answer accuracy, while a gap to the pass@4 ceiling remains under both conditions.

B.4 First Turn Wall Clock Time

We batch 256 questions in a single vLLM call and time the first turn under each method. Turns 2 through 8 issue one search per thread under both methods and have identical per-turn cost, so we benchmark turn 1 only.

Table 5 shows DivInit is slower at the 1.7B parameter scale, and faster at 4B and 8B. Standard runs k=4k{=}4 reasoning traces per question, each followed by a single query. In contrast, DivInit runs a single reasoning trace for n=16n{=}16 queries. At 4B and 8B, the kk-fold multiplier on the long reasoning trace dominates, and wall time tracks total tokens. Turns 2 through 8 dilute this turn-1 gap across the full eight-turn rollout.

Appendix C Case Studies

We present four trajectory-level case studies from GAIA experiments with Qwen3-8B at k=4k{=}4 and n=16n{=}16. Cases C and C show where DivInit succeeds while standard parallel sampling fails; Cases C and C show the reverse.
